idiom_name: module-private field + checked methods (newtype guard); pub(crate)/private visibility as the enclosure
implementation_notes: Rust enforces the pattern's core claim with the type system rather than with discipline: 'By default, everything is private' and a private item 'may be accessed by the current module and its descendants', so a public guard struct with a private resource field is genuinely unreachable outside its module - there is no reflection API that can name the field, and ownership means a reference can only leave if the guard's own code makes it public. The guard is therefore a newtype/module whose impl methods consult the policy before touching the resource; keep the module small, expose only these methods, and never implement Deref/AsRef to the resource, which would hand callers the whole API back. `unsafe` remains the escape hatch (transmute, raw pointers) and interior mutability (RefCell/RwLock) means the policy must be consulted on every mutable operation, not at construction. When the resource is a file, std's permissions API (PermissionsExt::mode/set_mode on Unix) exposes the mode bits that the OS enforces, which is the second layer for cross-process guarantees.
pitfalls: Do not implement Deref/DerefMut (or From/AsRef into the resource): deref coercion would hand callers the resource's whole API and re-open every path the guard closed.

pub(crate) is a real leak in a large crate: every module in the crate can name the field, so keep the guard in a small module and never widen visibility for a test helper (a #[cfg(test)] submodule is a descendant and already sees private items).
Interior mutability (RefCell/Mutex/RwLock) lets a shared &Vault mutate the resource, so each such operation needs its own policy check and a borrowed guard must not outlive the decision.

Returning &Store, cloning a cheap handle, or exposing the resource through a public trait method short-circuits the guard exactly like a getter; and unsafe code (transmute, raw pointers) bypasses module privacy entirely.
